title: Handley Page Halifax NR287
memorial_details:
1) Small bronze plaque on a wooden backboard, with dedication in raised upper-case letters. A Free French Cross of Lorraine is located above the text. / 2) A framed, explanatory scroll, headed by the Squadron badge, is located beneath the plaque.

The inscription mentions the plaque was attached to a tree against which the Halifax came to rest until it fell and the plaque was moved to the church porch here in Scawton.
inscription: Plaque: HERE ON MARCH 15th 1945 FELL/ A HALIFAX BOMBER RETURNING / FROM AN OPERATIONAL FLIGHT./ THE FOLLOWING MEMBERS/ OF THE CREW WERE KILLED./ (Names)/ Scroll: 347 (Tunisie) Sqn/ This plaque is a memorial to five Free French Airmen killed as they/ returned to their base at Elvington from their thirty eighth and last/ mission. Unable to land due to a build up of other returning aircraft they/ flew north to await their turn to land. HALIFAX NR 287 LB-C (Charles) fate/ was sealed when, with damaged instruments and zero visibility, it struck a/ stone wall strewing debris across the fields./ The Halifax spilled out two of its occupants as it slithered and bounced its/ way across the earth, it punched its way through another wall and/ became airborne for a few hundred yards before finally being brought rest/ against a tree on farmland about half a mile from this church. Only the/ Flight Engineer and Rear Gunner escaped, though badly injured from/ the wreckage. For some years the plaque was attached to the tree against/ which the Halifax came to rest until the tree fell and the plaque was/ removed to the church porch here in Scawton./ Lest we Forget

sources.title: Facebook post by Paul Goddard (RAF Bomber Command Memorials group) — confirms plaque moved from fallen tree to St Mary's, Scawton; photo by Paul Goddard; note on aircraft code

cause_of_loss: Damaged instruments and zero visibility on return; struck a stone wall; aircraft slid across fields and came to rest against a tree
narrative: On 15 March 1945, Halifax NR287 of 347 (Tunisie) Squadron, based at RAF Elvington, was returning from its crew's 38th and final mission when it could not land — other aircraft were stacking up over the airfield. The crew flew north to await their turn. With damaged instruments and zero visibility, the aircraft struck a stone wall, spilling two occupants as it slid across the fields; it punched through another wall, became airborne briefly, and came to rest against a tree on farmland about half a mile from Scawton Church. Five Free French airmen were killed; the flight engineer and rear gunner escaped though badly injured. For some years a plaque was fixed to the tree; when it fell, the plaque was moved to the church porch at St Mary's, Scawton. Note: the Facebook source gives aircraft code as 'LB-C'; 347 Squadron's official code was L8 — verify.
community_connection: The plaque's history reflects the village's ongoing stewardship: originally affixed to the tree where the Halifax came to rest, it was moved to St Mary's Church, Scawton, when the tree fell. The church has cared for the memorial ever since.
